First listed 2026-06-24 · episode or wrap

Why Cannabis Rescheduling Changes Everything for Glass House Brands

Jonathan DeCourcey argues that medical rescheduling can transform Glass House by opening higher-priced markets, lowering taxes and enabling a US listing. Eisman explicitly adopts the speculative margin thesis in his recap. The NYSE listing and first European hemp sale occurred, while the guest's pre-fall broad-rescheduling deadline failed. Export permits and state rules remain material, European cultivation already exists, and the proposed Medicare market is overstated. Eisman also converts a production-cost target into a current figure and confuses illustrative gross margin with operating margin. The larger earnings opportunity remains conditional.

Substack · 2026-06-24 ↗
The successful listing and hemp export are distinct from unproven interstate medical-cannabis economics. Guest errors are recorded separately; Eisman is responsible only for his explicit claims and closing adoption. The investment thesis remains unresolved, while its legal, cost and margin premises contain identifiable errors.

SPEAKER_01 is Steve Eisman and SPEAKER_00 is Jonathan DeCourcey, identified as Glass House head of investor relations. Very short interjections are occasionally embedded within the other speaker's segment; attribution follows the surrounding question and response.

  • DeCorsi is normalized to Jonathan DeCourcey from the identified company role.

  • The guest initially says target selling price then explicitly corrects to target production cost.
  • Eisman's closing operating-margin language differs from the guest's gross-margin calculation.
  • Publication follows June retail deconsolidation; original interview figures describe the earlier business perimeter.
  • The first completed European transaction was hemp; it is not evidence of unrestricted marijuana exports.

How he reasons here

  • Compare a restricted local market with potential expanded-market economics.
  • Separate current operations, installed capacity, targets and realized production.
  • Treat legal reform, licensing and distribution implementation as distinct milestones.
  • Use price-volume-cost scenarios while retaining incremental expenses.
  • Separate a successful exchange listing from investment returns and operating success.
  • Disclose ownership and distinguish speculative opportunity from modeled valuation.
